lessons.title: Types of Feedstocks: Manure, Crop Residues, Food Waste, Industrial Waste
lessons.body:
Biogas digesters need feedstock â organic material that bacteria break down to produce methane. In Africa, the most common feedstocks are animal manure, crop residues, food waste, and industrial waste. Each has different gas yields, handling needs, and costs. Choosing the right mix is key to a steady biogas supply.

Animal manure is the easiest feedstock for most small farms. Cattle dung from one cow produces about 0.5 to 1 cubic meter of biogas per day. Pig manure is richer â one pig gives about 0.2 to 0.4 mÂ³/day. Poultry litter is very strong but must be diluted with water (1 part litter to 3 parts water) to avoid ammonia poisoning of the bacteria. Fresh manure should be used within 2 days to avoid losing gas potential.

Crop residues include maize stalks, rice straw, groundnut shells, and banana peels. They are plentiful after harvest but are high in fibre (lignin), which digests slowly. To use them, chop or grind them to 2-5 cm pieces. A mix of 30% crop residues with 70% manure works well. Avoid diseased plants or those treated with pesticides.

Food waste from markets, restaurants, or homes is a high-energy feedstock. One kilogram of food waste can produce 0.5 to 0.8 mÂ³ of biogas. But it decomposes fast and can turn acidic, so add it in small daily amounts (no more than 20% of total feed). Remove bones, plastics, and oils â oils kill bacteria.

Industrial waste from breweries, palm oil mills, or abattoirs is very strong and often free. Brewery waste (spent grain) has high water content and produces 0.6-0.9 mÂ³ biogas per kg. Palm oil mill effluent (POME) is acidic (pH 4-5) and must be neutralised with lime or mixed with manure. Abattoir waste must be chopped and mixed with water. Always check with local authorities before using industrial waste â some may contain heavy metals or antibiotics.

Start with what you have locally. A mix of 60% manure, 20% food waste, and 20% crop residues gives good gas and stable digestion.

lessons.title: Characterizing Feedstocks: Total Solids, Volatile Solids, C/N Ratio
lessons.body:
To design a digester and predict biogas yield, you must know three key numbers: Total Solids (TS), Volatile Solids (VS), and Carbon-to-Nitrogen (C/N) ratio. You can measure TS and VS with simple tools: a kitchen scale, oven or sun-dryer, and a furnace or strong fire. C/N ratio needs a lab test or a chart.

Total Solids (TS) is the percentage of dry matter in a feedstock. For example, fresh cattle manure is about 15% TS, meaning 100 kg of manure contains 15 kg dry solids and 85 kg water. Pig manure is 5-8% TS, poultry litter 20-30% TS. To measure TS: weigh a sample (say 100 g), dry it at 105Â°C until weight stops changing (or sun-dry for 3 days in a thin layer). The dry weight divided by wet weight times 100 gives %TS. A digester needs a feed slurry of 8-12% TS. If your feedstock is too dry, add water; if too wet, add dry material like chopped straw.

Volatile Solids (VS) is the organic fraction of TS â the part bacteria can eat. For manure, VS is about 70-80% of TS. For food waste, VS is 85-95% of TS. To measure VS: burn the dried sample at 550Â°C (or in a very hot fire) until only ash remains. The weight lost is VS. High VS means more biogas potential. A typical cow manure has 0.2-0.3 mÂ³ biogas per kg VS.

C/N Ratio is the balance of carbon (energy) and nitrogen (protein) for bacteria. The ideal range is 20:1 to 30:1. Manure has C/N around 15-25 (good). Crop residues like maize stalks have C/N 40-60 (too high â add manure). Food waste has C/N 15-25. Poultry litter has C/N 10-15 (too low â add crop residues). If C/N is too high, bacteria grow slowly; too low, ammonia builds up and kills them. To adjust: mix high-C materials (straw, sawdust) with high-N materials (manure, food waste). For example, 1 part maize stalks (C/N 50) with 2 parts pig manure (C/N 15) gives a mix around 25:1.

Test your feedstock before feeding. Keep a notebook with TS, VS, and C/N for each batch. This helps you repeat good results.

lessons.title: Co-digestion: Benefits and Mixing Strategies
lessons.body:
Co-digestion means feeding two or more feedstocks together in one digester. It is the single best way to increase biogas yield and stability, especially for small African farms. Instead of relying on one material, you blend them to balance nutrients, moisture, and C/N ratio.

The benefits are many. First, higher gas yield: mixing manure with food waste can boost methane by 20-50% compared to manure alone. Second, better stability: manure provides buffering (alkalinity) that prevents acid build-up from food waste. Third, use of local waste: you can turn problem wastes (market scraps, crop residues) into energy. Fourth, year-round feed: when one feedstock is scarce (e.g., dry season manure), another is available (e.g., stored crop residues).

Mixing strategies depend on what you have. A simple rule: keep manure as the base (50-70% of feed) and add other materials in small amounts. For a 10 mÂ³ family digester, feed 50 kg fresh manure, 10 kg chopped food waste, and 5 kg ground crop residues daily. Mix with water to 10% TS. Another common mix: 60% cattle manure, 20% pig manure, 20% food waste. This gives C/N around 25:1 and TS around 10%.

Always test new mixes in a small bucket first. Fill a 20-litre bucket with the mix, keep it warm (25-35Â°C), and watch for 3 days. If it smells like rotten eggs or turns acidic (pH below 6.5), reduce the new material. If it smells like ammonia (urine), add more carbon-rich material like straw.

Avoid co-digesting with materials that contain antibiotics, pesticides, or heavy metals. Also avoid too much oil or fat â they coat bacteria and stop digestion. Citrus peels (orange, lemon) contain limonene, which kills bacteria; use no more than 5% of feed.

For best results, chop all feedstocks to 2-5 cm, mix thoroughly with water, and feed at the same time each day. Keep a record of what you feed and the gas pressure. After 2-3 weeks, you will know the best mix for your digester.

lessons.title: Pretreatment Methods: Mechanical, Thermal, Chemical, Biological
lessons.body:
Some feedstocks, especially crop residues and industrial waste, are hard for bacteria to digest. Pretreatment breaks down tough fibres (lignin, cellulose) so bacteria can work faster and produce more gas. There are four main methods: mechanical, thermal, chemical, and biological. Choose based on cost, available tools, and feedstock type.

Mechanical pretreatment is the simplest and most common in Africa. It means chopping, grinding, or crushing feedstock to increase surface area. For crop residues like maize stalks, chop to 2-5 cm with a machete or a motorised chipper. For hard materials like groundnut shells, grind them in a hammer mill. A simple hand grinder works for small amounts. Mechanical pretreatment can increase biogas yield by 10-20% and speed up digestion. It also prevents floating crusts in the digester.

Thermal pretreatment uses heat to break down fibres. You can heat feedstock to 70-100Â°C for 1-2 hours (pasteurisation) or use steam. In Africa, solar heating is practical: spread chopped residues in a black plastic bag under the sun for 2-3 days. This raises temperature to 60-80Â°C and softens fibres. For food waste, heating to 70Â°C for 1 hour kills pathogens and improves digestion. But thermal pretreatment requires energy; only use if you have free solar heat or waste heat from a generator.

Chemical pretreatment uses acids or bases. The cheapest is lime (calcium hydroxide) or wood ash. For crop residues, soak chopped material in a 1-2% lime solution for 24 hours, then rinse. This breaks lignin and increases gas yield by 20-30%. For acidic industrial waste like POME, add lime to raise pH to 6.5-7.5. Caution: chemicals can harm bacteria if not rinsed properly, and they add cost. Use only when needed.

Biological pretreatment uses fungi or enzymes to break down fibres. White-rot fungi (e.g., oyster mushroom spawn) can be mixed with crop residues and left for 1-2 weeks. This is slow but cheap and chemical-free. Another method is to let manure compost for a few days before feeding â natural bacteria start breaking down fibres. For most small farms, mechanical + biological (composting) is the best combination.

Always wear gloves and a mask when handling chemicals. Test pretreated feedstock in a small digester before scaling up.

lessons.title: Feedstock Storage and Handling Best Practices
lessons.body:
How you store and handle feedstock affects biogas yield, digester health, and your daily workload. Poor storage leads to loss of organic matter, bad smells, flies, and disease. Good practices are simple and low-cost.

Manure: Fresh manure gives the most gas. If you cannot feed it immediately, store it in a covered pit or under a plastic sheet to reduce ammonia loss and rain dilution. A concrete pit with a roof works well. Do not let manure dry out completely â 50-70% moisture is ideal. For daily feeding, collect manure each morning, mix with water to 10% TS, and feed. If you store for more than 3 days, add water and cover to keep anaerobic conditions. Avoid mixing manure with urine or bedding soaked in disinfectant â these kill bacteria.

Crop residues: Store dry and under cover. Maize stalks, rice straw, and groundnut shells should be kept in a dry shed or stacked under a tarpaulin. Moisture above 15% causes mould and rot, reducing gas potential. Before feeding, chop or grind. If you store chopped material, use it within 2 weeks. For long-term storage, keep whole and chop just before use. Never store residues in the open where rain can leach nutrients.

Food waste: This is the most challenging. It decomposes quickly and attracts pests. Collect food waste daily in sealed buckets. Separate bones, plastics, and oils. If you cannot feed immediately, store in a refrigerator or freeze â but that is expensive. A better option: dry food waste in the sun for 2-3 days, then store in sacks. Dried food waste can last 2-3 weeks. Alternatively, mix food waste with dry manure or sawdust to absorb moisture and reduce smell. Feed within 24 hours of collection if possible.

Industrial waste: Store according to its nature. Brewery waste (spent grain) must be used within 2-3 days or it spoils. Palm oil mill effluent (POME) is liquid and should be stored in a covered tank; it settles, so stir before feeding. Abattoir waste must be chilled or frozen if not used within 24 hours. Always check with the supplier for storage recommendations.

General rules: Keep a separate storage area for each feedstock. Label everything. Use gloves and boots when handling. Keep records of what you store and when. A simple notebook works. Train everyone on the farm to follow the same routine.

lessons.title: Case Study: Designing a Feedstock Mix for a Farm-Scale Digester
lessons.body:
This case study is based on a real 20 mÂ³ fixed-dome digester on a mixed farm in Kenya. The farm has 10 dairy cows, 20 pigs, and 2 acres of maize. The farmer wanted to produce enough biogas for cooking and lighting for a family of 8, and to use the bio-slurry as fertiliser.

Step 1: Inventory available feedstocks. Daily: cattle manure 100 kg (15% TS), pig manure 40 kg (6% TS), maize stalks after harvest 50 kg (80% TS, but only available 2 months per year), and food waste from the kitchen 5 kg (20% TS). The farmer also had access to free brewery waste (spent grain) from a nearby brewery, 20 kg per day (25% TS).

Step 2: Calculate TS and C/N. Using standard values: cattle manure C/N 20, pig manure C/N 15, maize stalks C/N 50, food waste C/N 20, spent grain C/N 12. The farmer wanted a mix with C/N 25 and 10% TS slurry.

Step 3: Design the mix. Base: 100 kg cattle manure + 40 kg pig manure gives 100*0.15 + 40*0.06 = 15 + 2.4 = 17.4 kg TS. Add 5 kg food waste (1 kg TS) and 20 kg spent grain (5 kg TS). Total TS = 23.4 kg. To get 10% TS slurry, add water to make total weight 234 kg (so add 234 - 165 = 69 kg water). This mix has C/N around: (100*20 + 40*15 + 5*20 + 20*12) / (100+40+5+20) = (2000+600+100+240)/165 = 2940/165 = 17.8. Too low. Add 10 kg maize stalks (8 kg TS, C/N 50) to raise C/N. New total TS = 31.4 kg, C/N = (2940 + 10*50)/(165+10) = 3440/175 = 19.7. Still low. Add 20 kg maize stalks: TS = 39.4 kg, C/N = (2940+1000)/185 = 21.3. Acceptable.

Step 4: Daily feeding. Final mix: 100 kg cattle manure, 40 kg pig manure, 5 kg food waste, 20 kg spent grain, 20 kg chopped maize stalks. Total fresh weight = 185 kg. Add water to reach 10% TS: total TS = 15+2.4+1+5+16 = 39.4 kg. Target slurry weight = 394 kg. Add 394 - 185 = 209 kg water. Mix well. Feed once daily.

Step 5: Results. After 3 months, the digester produced 4-5 mÂ³ biogas per day (enough for cooking 3 meals and 4 hours of light). Bio-slurry output was 200 kg per day, used on maize and vegetables. The farmer saved 50% on fertiliser costs. The key lesson: start with what you have, test small mixes, and adjust based on gas pressure and smell. Keep records.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feedstock Selection & Pretreatment for African Biogas Enterprises

This reference lesson consolidates the operational knowledge you need to source, test, store, and pretreat biogas feedstocks profitably in African conditions. It is written for the entrepreneur or farm manager who must make daily decisions about what goes into the digester â and what comes out as revenue. Every recommendation here is designed to protect your biogas yield, your equipment, and your margin.

1. The Business Case for Getting Feedstock Right

Feedstock typically represents 40â70% of the operating cost of a biogas plant. In sub-Saharan Africa, where grid electricity tariffs for small businesses range from USD 0.10â0.30/kWh and LPG is often imported, a well-designed feedstock mix can cut fuel costs by half. But poor feedstock choices destroy digesters: high-solids slurries clog pipes, ammonia from unbalanced C/N ratios kills methanogens, and sand or grit from unwashed manure abrades pumps. The discipline of feedstock selection is therefore a financial control, not just a technical one.

2. Types of Feedstocks Available in Africa

Animal manure (cattle, pig, poultry) is the backbone of most African digesters. Cattle slurry is abundant on mixed farms but low in energy density. Poultry litter is nitrogen-rich and must be co-digested carefully. Crop residues â maize stover, rice straw, cassava peels, banana pseudostems â are lignocellulosic and need pretreatment. Food waste from markets, hotels, and institutions is high-yield but variable and can carry plastics and pathogens. Industrial waste â abattoir effluent, brewery waste, palm oil mill effluent (POME), sisal pulp â is often the highest-yield and most consistent feedstock, and frequently available under waste-disposal contracts that generate tipping fees.

3. Characterizing Feedstocks: The Three Numbers That Matter

Before committing to a feedstock, you need three measurements: Total Solids (TS), Volatile Solids (VS), and the Carbon-to-Nitrogen (C/N) ratio. TS tells you how much dry matter is present; VS tells you how much of that dry matter is organic and therefore convertible to biogas. The C/N ratio determines whether your digester will be nitrogen-starved (slow) or ammonia-inhibited (dead).

4. Data Table 1: Typical Feedstock Characteristics

Table 1: Typical TS, VS, C/N, and Biogas Yield of Common African Feedstocks

Sources: FAO Biogas Technology: A Practical Guide (2019); Global Methane Initiative Anaerobic Digestion Systems (2021); IEA Bioenergy Task 37 Biogas Handbook (2020).

5. Co-digestion: The Yield Multiplier

Co-digestion â feeding two or more substrates together â is the single most powerful lever for improving biogas yield and financial return. It balances C/N ratios, dilutes inhibitors, and smooths supply variability. The classic African combination is cattle manure (low C/N, buffering) plus maize stover or food waste (high C/N, high yield). A 70:30 manure-to-food-waste mix by VS can raise methane yield by 30â60% compared with manure alone.

Mixing strategies: Target a combined C/N ratio of 20â30:1. Keep the mix within 8â12% TS for liquid digesters and 20â30% TS for solid-state systems. Introduce new substrates gradually over 2â4 weeks to let the microbial community adapt. Never exceed 20% of VS from a single novel substrate in the first month.

6. Pretreatment Methods

Mechanical: Chopping, grinding, and maceration reduce particle size and increase surface area. A hammer mill or chaff cutter is the most cost-effective pretreatment for crop residues in Africa. Target 2â5 mm particle size.

Thermal: Heating to 70â120Â°C (pasteurization) kills pathogens and improves hydrolysis of lignocellulose. Solar thermal preheating is viable in most of Africa and can cut energy cost.

Chemical: Alkali treatment (NaOH, lime, or urea) breaks lignin bonds. Lime (Ca(OH)â) at 2â5% w/w is cheap and widely available. Ammonia soaking (urea) also adds nitrogen.

Biological: Fungal or enzymatic pretreatment (white-rot fungi, cellulases) is slow but low-cost. Composting or ensiling before digestion is a practical biological pretreatment for crop residues.

7. Data Table 2: Pretreatment CostâBenefit Comparison

Table 2: Pretreatment Methods â Cost, Yield Gain, and Suitability
Method Typical Cost (USD/tonne) Yield Gain Best For African Suitability

Chemical (lime/NaOH)5â1520â40%Lignocellulosic residuesHigh â lime locally available
Biological (fungal/ensiling)1â510â30%Crop residues, strawHigh â low capital, slow
Combined (mechanical + chemical)10â2530â55%Straw, stover, sisal pulpMedium â needs training

Sources: IEA Bioenergy Task 37 Pretreatment of Feedstocks for Anaerobic Digestion (2020); FAO Bioenergy and Food Security Rapid Appraisal (2019); African Development Bank Bioenergy Investment Framework (2022).

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Hydrogen Sulphide (HâS) and Ammonia Hazards

Biogas from high-nitrogen feedstocks (poultry litter, abattoir waste) contains hydrogen sulphide (HâS) at concentrations that can cause rapid unconsciousness and death in confined spaces. Never enter a digester, storage tank, or pit without a calibrated HâS monitor, forced ventilation, and a standby person outside. Ammonia released during storage of poultry litter and food waste can also cause severe respiratory burns. Store high-nitrogen feedstocks in ventilated, covered areas away from livestock and workers. Always wear gloves, goggles, and a respirator when handling lime or NaOH during chemical pretreatment.

8. Feedstock Storage and Handling Best Practices

In African conditions, feedstock quality degrades quickly. Store manure under cover to prevent rain dilution and nutrient leaching. Ensile or dry crop residues to below 20% moisture to prevent mould. Keep food waste in sealed, cool containers and feed within 48 hours. Industrial waste should be piped directly from source where possible. Always maintain a 3â7 day buffer stock to protect against supply interruptions â a common risk during rainy season or harvest peaks.

9. Case Study: Designing a Feedstock Mix for a Farm-Scale Digester

Scenario: A 50-cow dairy farm in Kiambu County, Kenya, installs a 30 mÂ³ fixed-dome digester to supply cooking gas for 12 staff and to produce biofertilizer for 5 hectares of fodder. The farm has access to cattle manure, maize stover from neighbouring farms, and food waste from a nearby market.

Design: The mix is 60% cattle manure, 25% maize stover (chopped to 3 mm, lime-treated at 3% w/w), and 15% food waste by VS. The combined C/N ratio is 24:1, TS is 10%, and predicted biogas yield is 0.32 mÂ³/kg VS. Daily feed is 180 kg of mixed slurry, producing approximately 9 mÂ³ of biogas â enough for 6 hours of cooking and 3 hours of lighting. Digestate is applied to fodder plots, replacing 40% of purchased NPK.

Result: Payback period is 2.8 years. The farm saves USD 1,200/year on LPG and USD 600/year on fertilizer. The key success factor was consistent feedstock testing and gradual introduction of stover over 6 weeks.

10. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test every new feedstock for TS, VS, and C/N before committing to a supply contract.
  2. Target a combined C/N ratio of 20â30:1 and TS of 8â12% for liquid digesters.
  3. Co-digest at least two substrates to buffer supply and improve yield.
  4. Pretreat lignocellulosic residues mechanically (2â5 mm) and consider lime or urea.
  5. Store manure and food waste under cover; ensile or dry crop residues below 20% moisture.
  6. Maintain 3â7 days of buffer feedstock to survive supply interruptions.
  7. Never enter a digester or pit without HâS monitoring and forced ventilation.
  8. Track biogas yield weekly and adjust the mix based on measured performance, not assumptions.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Biogas Technology: A Practical Guide (2019)
  • Global Methane Initiative â Anaerobic Digestion Systems Handbook (2021)
  • IEA Bioenergy Task 37 â Biogas Handbook (2020)
  • African Development Bank â Bioenergy Investment Framework (2022)
  • IRENA â Bioenergy for Heat and Power: Africa Focus (2021)

quiz.q: Which feedstock produces the most biogas per kilogram?
quiz.explanation: Food waste has high volatile solids and can produce 0.5-0.8 mÂ³ biogas per kg, more than manure or crop residues.

quiz.q: What is the ideal Total Solids (TS) percentage for a digester feed slurry?
quiz.explanation: A slurry of 8-12% TS allows bacteria to move and digest efficiently without being too thick or too watery.

quiz.q: Which material has a very high C/N ratio and should be mixed with manure?
quiz.explanation: Maize stalks have C/N around 40-60, which is too high; mixing with low C/N manure balances the ratio.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of co-digestion?
options: A) It reduces the need for water
B) It increases biogas yield and stability
quiz.explanation: Co-digestion balances nutrients and C/N, leading to higher methane production and a more stable digester.

quiz.q: Which pretreatment method involves soaking feedstock in a lime solution?
quiz.explanation: Lime (calcium hydroxide) is a chemical that breaks down lignin and improves digestion.

quiz.q: How should fresh manure be stored if not used immediately?
options: A) In an open pile under the sun
B) In a covered pit or under plastic
quiz.explanation: Covering reduces ammonia loss and rain dilution, preserving biogas potential.

quiz.q: What is the ideal C/N ratio for anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: Bacteria need a balance of carbon and nitrogen; 20:1 to 30:1 is optimal for growth and gas production.

quiz.q: Which of these should be avoided in feedstock because it kills bacteria?
options: B) Citrus peels in large amounts
quiz.explanation: Citrus peels contain limonene, which is toxic to methanogens; use no more than 5% of feed.

quiz.q: What does Volatile Solids (VS) measure?
options: B) The organic fraction that bacteria can digest
quiz.explanation: VS is the portion of total solids that is organic and can be converted to biogas.

quiz.q: Which pretreatment method is best for a small farm with no electricity?
options: A) Mechanical chopping with a machete
B) Thermal heating with a furnace
quiz.explanation: Mechanical chopping is low-cost, requires no energy, and is effective for most crop residues.

quiz.q: What is the recommended particle size for chopped crop residues before feeding?
quiz.explanation: Chopping to 2-5 cm increases surface area for bacteria without being too fine, which can cause clogging.

quiz.q: Which feedstock is very acidic and must be neutralised before feeding?
quiz.explanation: POME has pH 4-5, which is too acidic for methanogens; lime or mixing with manure raises pH.

quiz.q: How can you test if a new feedstock mix is safe for your digester?
options: A) Feed it directly and watch for 3 days
B) Test in a small bucket for 3 days
D) Add it to the digester without testing
quiz.explanation: A small bucket test allows you to observe pH, smell, and gas production before scaling up.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of adding too much oil or fat to a digester?
options: B) It coats bacteria and stops digestion
C) It makes the slurry too dry
quiz.explanation: Oils and fats form a layer on bacteria, preventing them from accessing nutrients.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biological pretreatment method?
options: A) Chopping with a hammer mill
C) Composting with manure for a few days
quiz.explanation: Composting allows natural bacteria and fungi to partially break down fibres before feeding.

quiz.q: What percentage of total feed should food waste ideally not exceed?
quiz.explanation: Food waste decomposes fast and can acidify the digester; keeping it below 20% maintains stability.

quiz.q: Why should manure be used within 2 days of collection?
options: B) It loses biogas potential as it decomposes aerobically
quiz.explanation: Aerobic decomposition consumes organic matter that would otherwise produce methane in the digester.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding water to feedstock before feeding?
options: B) To adjust Total Solids to 8-12%
quiz.explanation: Water dilutes the slurry to the optimal TS range for bacterial movement and digestion.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that a feedstock mix is too acidic?
quiz.explanation: A pH below 6.5 indicates acid build-up, which inhibits methanogens; add buffering material like manure.

quiz.q: What is the best storage method for dried food waste?
options: A) In sealed buckets with water
B) In sacks in a dry place
quiz.explanation: Drying and storing in sacks prevents spoilage and reduces smell for up to 2-3 weeks.

quiz.q: Which feedstock has the lowest C/N ratio?
quiz.explanation: Poultry litter has C/N around 10-15, which is too low and can cause ammonia toxicity if used alone.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of thermal pretreatment using solar heat?
options: A) It is free and kills pathogens
quiz.explanation: Solar heating is low-cost, uses renewable energy, and can pasteurise feedstock while softening fibres.

quiz.q: How much biogas can one cow produce per day?
quiz.explanation: A typical cow produces enough dung for 0.5-1 mÂ³ of biogas daily under good conditions.

quiz.q: Which industrial waste is commonly available from breweries?
quiz.explanation: Breweries produce spent grain, a high-energy feedstock with 25% TS and C/N around 12.

quiz.q: What should you do if your digester smells like rotten eggs?
options: B) Reduce the new material and check pH
D) Stop feeding for a week
quiz.explanation: Rotten egg smell indicates acid build-up or sulfur; reduce problematic feedstock and monitor pH.

quiz.q: What is the target moisture content for stored manure?
quiz.explanation: 50-70% moisture keeps manure anaerobic and preserves organic matter for digestion.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended practice for feedstock handling?
quiz.explanation: Random mixing can lead to poor C/N or TS; always measure and test before feeding.

quiz.q: In the case study, what was the final C/N ratio of the mix?
quiz.explanation: After adding maize stalks, the calculated C/N was 21.3, within the acceptable range.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of mechanical pretreatment?
options: B) It increases surface area for faster digestion
quiz.explanation: Chopping or grinding reduces particle size, allowing bacteria to access more organic matter quickly.

quiz.q: Which feedstock should be used with caution because it may contain antibiotics?
options: A) Cattle manure from a dairy
B) Pig manure from a commercial farm
quiz.explanation: Commercial pig farms often use antibiotics in feed, which can end up in manure and inhibit digester bacteria.
